transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

Here is what I understood, and one thing I checked before saying anything.

**The problem as I see it.** Every month you commit guide capacity for a travel month that is two months away, and the cost of being short is far bigger than the cost of being spare. Your director asked for a bookings forecast; what actually saves you money is a reservation number per destination, with a band you can deliberately aim high inside. Your export can support that: 1,500 bookings, booked 2025-01-01 to 2026-02-24, across Paris (317), Bangkok (304), Dubai (302), London (283) and Istanbul (282).

**Three things that need care before any model is built.**

1. *The look-ahead trap.* Counting bookings per travel month from the full export is not what you know on decision day. A model trained on the finished month and asked to predict the finished month looks superb in testing and fails at your desk. It must be trained only on what was visible then.
2. *Bookings are not guides.* The table has no bookings-per-guide conversion, so I can forecast bookings but cannot hand you a guide count until you tell me the ratio. Also, cancellations run 18.9% to 26.2% by destination, so guides should follow **net, non-cancelled** bookings, not gross. And because your costs are lopsided, a single "best guess" average is the wrong output — you need a high quantile, chosen from your cost ratio.
3. *Two data notes.* 12 rows are labelled destination "TEST" (I assume test records, to be dropped with your OK). And free cancellation makes no difference to cancelling — 23.3% versus 22.6% — which I would not expect, so I will treat that flag as unreliable for now. History covers roughly 12 clean travel months, one seasonal cycle, so seasonality gets pooled across destinations rather than learned per destination.

**The plan**

1. **Prepare the table** — drop TEST rows, parse both dates, tag each booking with its travel month and whether it would have been visible at a decision date two months ahead. Checked by row counts before/after, shown to you before anything is applied.
2. **Build the ground truth** — net confirmed bookings per destination per travel month, plus the share of each month already booked at decision date. Checked by tying totals back to the export and by your eye: "yes, that is my March".
3. **Set the yardstick** — a no-model baseline: open book at decision date, scaled by the historical completion rate. Every later number is judged against it, and against your cost shape (short versus spare), not just average error.
4. **Train the forecast** — pooled across destinations, using only decision-day-visible features (open book, lead-time curve, channel and nationality mix, month), backtested month by month on real past decision dates. Checked by beating the baseline on backtest, and by a leakage check on every column.
5. **Turn it into a reservation** — pick the band from your cost ratio and translate to guides with your bookings-per-guide figure. Checked by comparing backtested cost of the model against the baseline.
6. **Run it monthly** — one refreshed page per destination you can send to your director.

Stop when: the model beats the open-book baseline on every backtested decision month and gives you a reservation number per destination you would actually send.
If a step fails: with only one year of history, step 4 may not beat the baseline — then we keep the open-book rule with a cost-sized buffer as your monthly method, and say plainly to your director what history would change that.

The three ways to start are on screen: the reservation model (my recommendation, and its first step is the open-book analysis anyway), the open-book rule alone today, or the monthly dashboard. Two numbers from you when we get there: how many bookings one reserved guide covers, and roughly how big the unused-guide fee is next to a guide's normal rate.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

transcript.text: I am the head of marketing at a subscription company. The board asked for an AI segmentation of our customers, and I would like five or six segments with names we can put on a slide. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, the segment we already record, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. Next quarter my team can run at most three email campaigns: one to move people to a higher plan, one to keep people who look likely to leave, and one welcome series for new customers. The same person should not receive two of them. My campaign managers will use the segments to decide who gets which campaign. [shares customers.csv]

Two more checks before I write the plan: the brand-new customers and any missing churn flags.

Understood — and your table backs the plan up. Here's what I take you to need.

**The problem.** The board wants 5–6 named segments, but the real decision is smaller and sharper: three email lists next quarter that cannot overlap, handable to your campaign managers without a statistics translation step. So the segments are only worth having if each one points at exactly one campaign, or at none. Good news: the segment you already record has just two values (consumer 961, business 239), so it genuinely cannot produce five or six groups — this work adds something.

**What needs care before we start.**
- `churned_next_month` is in your table for all 1,200 customers (209 yes). It must be the referee, not an ingredient: at send time you don't know it about a live customer. If it goes into the clustering, the segments will look brilliantly predictive and then fail in the field. I'll use it only to validate and size each segment afterwards.
- Upgrade and retention pull on the same people. basic is both your largest plan (603) and your leakiest (22.4% vs 11.1% on plus), and the newest basic customers churn at 27.0%. And premium churns *more* than plus, so "spends more" is not "safer". Anyone with a high-value, unhappy profile qualifies for both campaigns; a rule must decide, and that rule is a business choice, not a math one. My default: welcome first (it's time-critical), then retention, then upgrade.

**The plan**

1. **Cluster on what you know today**: tenure, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, plan, recorded segment. Output 5–6 groups, no outcome column touched.
2. **Name and size them** for the slide: each with a plain-language name, headcount, average spend, average tenure, average tickets.
3. **Validate against churn**: show each segment's actual `churned_next_month` rate beside the 17.4% overall. A segment is only kept if it separates — and if the new segments are not just a relabel of `plan`.
4. **Map to campaigns with a priority order**: welcome (newest by signup date), retention (highest-churn segments), upgrade (high-spend, low-ticket headroom on basic/plus), remainder gets nothing. One row per customer with one campaign tag, checked so no customer appears twice.
5. **Deliver**: a slide-ready segment table plus a per-customer assignment file your managers can filter, with the expected churn and spend for each list.

**Stop when** the three lists are non-overlapping, sized, and each segment's churn rate is shown to differ from 17.4% — and every segment has one campaign owner.
**If a step fails** (segments don't separate on churn, or they mirror `plan`), we switch to the churn-score route below rather than putting weak clusters on the slide.

I checked your table for leaky columns: no other field looks like it was written after the outcome, so the inputs are clean.

My pick is the first one: it gives the board exactly five or six named segments, and it ends with three lists that cannot overlap, which is what your managers actually need next quarter. The churn-score route is the right second step if you later want the retention list ranked rather than taken whole — and if you'd rather not wait for clustering at all, the rule-based version gets names and headcounts on a slide today.

Choose one and I'll run it; if you say "you decide", I'll start with the behavioural segmentation.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a company that sells accounting software to small firms. Two years ago we built a model that scores every new lead on how likely it is to become a customer, and the sales team calls the highest scores first. Since the autumn the sales team says the top leads are much worse than they used to be, and my manager wants me to retrain with a larger model and more features. Some context on the data: since the summer, part of our leads comes from a partner marketplace; we moved to a new CRM in August, and two form fields the model uses are no longer collected; and finance now counts a lead as converted when a free trial starts, where before it was the first payment. I have the old training set and every lead since, not yet exported. What would you do?

You've handed me a genuinely well-stated problem, and I think the diagnosis is mostly already in your paragraph — you just can't see which of your four changes is doing the damage. That's the real task, not the model size.

**What I think is going on.** Three of your four changes move the goalposts rather than the model. The label definition changed (trial start instead of first payment), so any conversion rate you compute across the boundary is two different numbers wearing one name. The marketplace changed who the leads are. The CRM migration changed what got recorded about them. And the model is still consuming two fields nobody collects since August — which means today's "bad" scores may partly be scores computed on imputed or default values, a plumbing failure, not a learning failure. A larger model with more features cannot recover fields you stopped capturing, and it cannot fix a target that means two things. It would, however, train very confidently on all of it.

**What needs care before any work starts.** Two things. First, retraining on labels produced under the current policy bakes in who your sales team chose to call — you only observe outcomes for leads someone dialled, so a model trained on that learns to imitate last year's queue order, including its mistakes. Second, and more urgent: before you conclude the model got worse, you need to confirm the world didn't just get measured differently. "Since autumn" lines up with August and with the label change. Any number you show your manager must hold one definition of converted fixed across time, or the drop you report may be an artefact of the definition, and a rebuild would be justified by nothing.

**Ways it could be solved.** *Diagnose first*: freeze a single outcome, slice by cohort, source and CRM era, and check whether the old model's ranking still holds up — cheap, days, and it's the only route that tells you whether your manager is right. *Rebuild target then model*: define conversion as a two-stage outcome and retrain on post-change leads with surviving features — clean, but much less history and no answer on whether the drop was real. *Fix the plumbing first*: one reconciled table both analyses and training runs read. I'd lead with the diagnosis, which forces the reconciled export anyway.

**The plan**

1. Write the export spec: every lead since the old training window, carrying source, CRM era, score at scoring time, both label versions, and the two discontinued fields' last-known values. Checked by: row counts per month and per source summing to total leads.
2. Freeze one outcome definition and compute base rates by month, split by source. Checked by: the pre-August rate matching the old model's training documents.
3. Rank-quality check: does the old score still separate converters from non-converters, by era and source? Same frozen label throughout.
4. Feature-integrity check: coverage and distribution of the two dropped fields, and what the live model does when they're absent.
5. Verdict: population shift, label shift, or genuine model decay — then choose the rebuild, with the target the evidence supports.

Stop when one of those three explains the share of the drop you can attribute; don't retrain before then.
If a step fails, it usually means the export lacks source or era tags — in that case I'd split by CRM record-ID range as a proxy and say so plainly.

My options got held back until two things are clear, and both live in the export you haven't pulled yet.

So one question, with two halves: when you export every lead since the old training window, **does the historical set now carry one definition of "converted" or two** (did finance restate old rows to trial-start, or do pre-change rows still mean first payment)? And **can that export carry a lead-source tag plus the old and new CRM keys**, so marketplace leads and the August migration can be told apart instead of inferred from dates?

Your answers decide whether we pool two years of data or start the clock at the label change — and that changes everything downstream.

Two halves of one question, both about what your export can contain: (1) Does the historical training set now carry ONE definition of converted, or TWO — did finance retroactively restate old rows to trial-start, or do pre-change rows still mean first payment? (2) Can the export carry a lead-source tag (marketplace vs direct) plus the old and new CRM record keys, so the August migration and the new channel can be separated rather than inferred from dates?
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

**Step 1 — the export spec.** Here is what to hand engineering. Grain: one row per lead, from the start of the old training window to today. **Identity and cohort.** `lead_id` (stable internal key), `crm_legacy_id` and `crm_new_id` (both, nulls allowed), `created_at`, `source_channel` plus `source_channel_raw` — and if channel is missing on some rows, keep them null; don't blank-fill, because a filled-in "direct" hides the gap. **Outcomes as raw dates, not a flag.** `trial_start_date`, `first_payment_date`, `current_status`, `amount_at_first_payment`, `cancel_date`. This is how I'm getting past the question you couldn't answer: no single `converted` column. With both dates in the file we freeze whichever definition we want per row, and whether finance restated history becomes visible immediately — if `trial_start_date` is empty for all pre-August leads, history was never restated, and we know exactly which rows are comparable. **Scoring.** `score_value`, `score_datetime`, `score_model_version`, and the feature snapshot the model actually received. **The two discontinued fields.** Export them with their values as stored, including any sentinel the pipeline wrote after August. A null tells us the data vanished; a median or "-1" tells us the model was fed a fake value — which is a plumbing failure, not drift, and the cheapest fix on this list. **Sales action.** `first_call_date`, `call_count`, `disposition`, `worked_flag`. This is the part people skip and the part that decides whether a retrain is even valid: if you only have outcomes for leads someone dialled, a new model learns to imitate last year's queue order, its mistakes included. Six checks I'll run before any modelling: row counts by month × channel summing to total leads; distinct `lead_id` equals row count (migrations duplicate leads); share of pre-August leads carrying a trial date; score coverage by month and version; null-rate by column before versus after August; and how many leads exist in both CRMs. Assumptions I've adopted, correct me if any is wrong: history wasn't restated; "worse" means fewer top leads reaching payment (the export tests the other reading too); the calling rule is unchanged; and if scores aren't logged, I'll rescore retroactively with the frozen model and label that evidence weaker. Run that export and drop the file here (CSV or Parquet) — I'll do step 2, base rates by month split by channel, on it straight away. Nothing retrains until the diagnosis names which of the four changes actually moved the number.

transcript.text: I am the credit risk manager at a consumer lender that finances phone and appliance purchases in shops. Today a rulebook written by our underwriters approves about 40 percent of applications. Management wants to grow, so they asked me for a machine learning model that predicts default for every applicant, to replace the rulebook and approve more people safely. We have about 60,000 past loans with the application form, the bureau score and whether the loan defaulted within 12 months, and I can export them next week. For the applications we rejected we kept the form and the bureau score, nothing more. The model would decide each new application automatically at the shop counter. How should I go about it?

[DCLab drew a dashboard above this message]

I'll set out the plan, then do its first step now — a blueprint you can hand to whoever builds the export, since your real risk (rejected applicants have no outcome) has to be designed around before a single row arrives.

Understood, and I want to name the one thing that makes this harder than it looks before anything gets built.

**The problem as you've described it is really two problems glued together.** The stated one: score every applicant's 12-month default risk, replace the rulebook, approve more. The actual decision it serves: how much wider to open the gate at the shop counter, and where to put the cut so the extra volume earns more than the extra losses. You own the loss rate; management owns the growth target.

**What needs care, and it needs care before your export is cut.** The 60,000 loans are the 40 percent the rulebook already judged acceptable. For the applications we rejected we kept the form and the bureau score, nothing more — so not one rejected applicant has an outcome. A model trained on that 60,000 learns "who defaults *given a rulebook already said yes*," and you are asking it to score the population it has never seen. Two consequences: its accuracy numbers will look better than its real-world performance, and the default rate you measure today is not what you will get on a wider mix. "Default rate" means different things for those two groups, and that is where portfolios get mispriced. The second issue is that this model decides automatically, at a counter, with adverse-action implications: an applicants' reason, plus fairness testing, since phone and appliance financing in shops concentrates thin-file and lower-income customers, and shop or geography features can quietly proxy for protected characteristics. A black-box score that says no with no reason is a governance problem, not a modelling one.

**Ways it could be solved.**
- Train on the 60,000 and swap it in. Fastest, and the one I would not do — the bias above is unbaked-in, and you have no estimate for the rejected zone at all.
- Score in the shadow of the rulebook first. Model ranks every application, rulebook still decides, and you approve a small deliberate slice of near-the-cut applicants the rulebook would have refused. Costs three to six months and a controlled, budgeted loss; it buys real labels for exactly the gray zone that matters, while growth continues.
- Reject-inference modelling now. Use the rejected applications' form and bureau score, and the bureau score's own relationship to default on the funded book, to estimate default in the rejected zone. Cheaper and faster, but rests on assumptions you can't verify.
- Model as a policy, not a replacement: keep the rulebook as a hard floor, and let the model set the cut to maximize approved volume subject to a bad-rate ceiling and a loss budget you and management agree.

My choice: shadow-score with a small randomized approve band near the cut, in a form that stays explainable (scorecard or monotonic boosted model with reason codes), and reject inference as the interim estimate for the first cut. The obvious reading of your brief — train and swap — is not the one I'd recommend.

**The plan**
1. Lock the outcome definition with you: days-past-due threshold, and how you treat accounts still open at 12 months, early payoffs, and re-finance. Checked against your servicing data; without this the target moves under you.
2. Agree the economics: what a default costs versus what an approved-and-repaid loan earns. That single ratio sets the cut, not an accuracy metric.
3. Cut the export to the minimum viable spec in the blueprint: one row per application, application date, all form fields *as captured at decision time*, bureau score as loaded that day, the rulebook's decision and its reasons, loan amount, and outcome with the maturity date. Plus the rejected applications' rows so the score distributions can be compared.
4. Baseline first: bureau score alone, scored on your funded book, split by time (train on older, test on a later period never used for tuning) — this is the number the model must beat, and the honest reference for the rejected zone.
5. Compare form + bureau vs bureau alone on the funded book; check drift month by month; check leakage from any post-decision field.
6. Design the shadow run and the approve band: what slice you deliberately accept, its loss budget, and how disagreements with the rulebook are logged.
7. Fairness and reason-code review before any applicant is affected automatically; sign-off from whoever owns compliance.
8. Champion/challenger switch, only when the shadow numbers hold.

**Stop when:** the model beats bureau-score-alone on a time-lagged test, gives a defensible cut for a loss budget management has approved, and can state a reason per adverse decision.
**If a step fails:** at step 4 or 5, the honest answer is that the rejected population is unmeasurable today — then the decision becomes "buy labels with a small approve band" rather than "swap the rulebook."

I've written the blueprint: the business case, the data spec to hand whoever does the export next week, the leakage traps to design around, and the pre-data task order. One caution: it had no economics from you, so the default rate, action cost, value per approved loan and the success rate of intervention are **placeholders DCLab filled by default — do not quote those numbers** until we replace them.

To set the cut, I need two figures from you: roughly what does a 12-month default cost you net of recovery, and roughly what do you earn on a loan that performs?

Chosen and going ahead.
